units.name: glob-matching
units.role: Compiles gitignore/shell-style glob patterns into an efficient matcher and tests candidate file paths against them.
units.description: This unit understands the language of file-matching wildcards, such as '*.rs' or '!foo/**', that people use to say which files they care about or want to skip. It takes a pattern written as text, checks that it is valid, and turns it into a fast internal matcher. It can also hold many patterns at once and quickly tell you which of them match a given file path. It is purely a text/pattern-matching brain: it never opens files, never walks directories, and never touches the network or the clock -- it just answers the yes/no (or which-ones) question 'does this path match these patterns' as fast as possible, leaving the job of finding files and deciding what to do with them to other parts of the program.

units.name: match-contract
units.role: Defines the shared vocabulary and rules for what it means to "search bytes for a pattern" that every concrete search engine and consumer in ripgrep agrees on.
units.description: This unit does not itself search anything. Instead, it defines the common language that all of ripgrep's pattern-matching engines (the default regex engine and the optional PCRE2 engine) and all of the code that uses them (the line searcher, the result printer) agree to speak. It says what a 'match' looks like (a start and end position in the text), what it means to ask an engine to find matches or capture groups, and how to fill in a replacement string like '$1' or '${name}' with the text a capture group actually matched. Because every regex engine in the project implements this same contract, the rest of the program can work with any of them interchangeably without needing to know which one is actually running.

entrypoints.name: Matcher
entrypoints.plain: The core interface every regex/substring engine implements; implemented by the regex and pcre2 units, called by the search-engine and output-printer units.

entrypoints.name: Match
entrypoints.signature: pub struct Match { start: usize, end: usize }
entrypoints.plain: A simple 'this match starts here and ends here' value.

entrypoints.plain: Turns a replacement pattern like '$1' or '${name}' into actual matched text, for the -r/--replace feature.

units.name: regex-matcher
units.role: Compiles a user's search pattern(s) and ripgrep-specific flags into a working matcher backed by Rust's default regex engine, and derives optimization hints from the compiled pattern.
units.description: This unit turns the text pattern a user types (plus options like 'ignore case' or 'match whole words') into a ready-to-use pattern matcher. It parses the pattern, applies ripgrep's rules about how those options should change the pattern's meaning, and hands back an object that can find matches in a chunk of text. It also analyzes the compiled pattern to help ripgrep search faster later: finding short pieces of text that must appear near any match, and figuring out which single characters can never be part of a match. This unit never opens a file, never reads from disk or the network, and never decides which files to search -- it only turns a pattern and a set of options into a matcher plus metadata about that matcher.

entrypoints.name: RegexMatcherBuilder
entrypoints.plain: Configures case sensitivity, word/line boundaries, fixed strings, multiline, crlf, and unicode options before building a matcher.

entrypoints.name: RegexMatcherBuilder::build

entrypoints.plain: Compiles a pattern string into a usable RegexMatcher.

entrypoints.plain: Convenience constructor for building a matcher directly from a pattern string.

units.name: pcre2-matcher
units.role: Alternate regex-engine backend that adapts the external PCRE2 C library to ripgrep's internal Matcher contract, enabled behind the -P/--pcre2 flag.
units.description: This unit lets ripgrep optionally search using PCRE2, a widely used regular-expression library written in C, instead of its own built-in Rust regex engine. It does not implement new pattern-matching logic itself; it is a thin translation layer that takes ripgrep's search configuration (case sensitivity, whole-word/whole-line matching, unicode mode, multiline mode, JIT settings) and configures the PCRE2 library accordingly, exposing the results in the same shape the rest of ripgrep already expects. This is what allows ripgrep to support advanced regex features like backreferences and lookaround, at the cost of requiring the PCRE2 C library to be available.

entrypoints.name: RegexMatcher

units.name: file-walker
units.role: Recursively traverses a directory tree and decides, file by file and directory by directory, which entries are candidates to search, by combining gitignore-style rules, explicit overrides, and file-type filters.
units.description: This is the part of ripgrep that answers the question 'which files and folders should actually be looked at?' It walks through a starting folder and all of its subfolders, and for each item it decides whether to skip it (because it's hidden, because it's excluded by a .gitignore file or similar rule, because it's the wrong file type, because it's a symlink loop, or because it crosses onto a different disk) or to include it in the list of things to search. It understands the layered, override-based precedence rules that .gitignore and .ignore files use, including global git config and per-directory files, and it can walk on a single thread or spread the work across a pool of threads for speed. It must never silently search files a user has told it to ignore, and must never report a file/directory cycle as an infinite traversal.

entrypoints.name: Walk

units.name: search-engine
units.role: Drives the core read-search-report loop: pulls bytes from a file/mmap/slice/reader, splits into lines, applies a Matcher, handles multiline and binary detection, and pushes results to a Sink.
units.description: This is the engine at the heart of ripgrep that actually performs a search once a file (or other byte source) and a pattern-matcher have been chosen. It reads the data in manageable chunks (growing its buffer as needed, or memory-mapping the file when configured), breaks the data into lines, hands each chunk to the matcher to ask 'does this match?', and for every match or requested context line it calls back into a caller-supplied Sink to report what was found. It also handles special cases: matches that span multiple lines, binary-data detection, line numbering, match limits, and encoding transcoding. It must never decide what pattern to look for and must never decide how results are displayed -- it only decides how to walk the bytes and when to call the sink.

units.name: output-printer
units.role: Formats search results (matches, context lines, and statistics) received from the search engine into the standard colored text, JSON-lines, or per-file summary formats ripgrep can emit, including terminal hyperlinks.
units.description: This unit is responsible for turning raw search results into something a person or another program can read. When ripgrep finds a match in a file, this code decides how to display it: as classic colored grep-style output with line numbers, as a JSON stream that other tools can parse, or as a short per-file summary with counts. It also tracks statistics like how many matches and files were seen and how long the search took, and it can turn file paths into clickable links in terminals that support them. It does not search files or decide which files to look at; it only takes results that were already found and presents them.

units.name: trigram-index
units.role: Builds and reads an optional, opt-in on-disk trigram index of a directory's contents so that a later search can skip files that provably cannot match, and derives the required trigram query from a regex pattern.
units.description: This is an experimental, off-by-default feature that lets ripgrep remember, ahead of time, small fragments of text ('trigrams') found in each file of a directory, storing that memory in a hidden database file on disk. When a later search runs, ripgrep can look at which fragments the search pattern must contain and consult this stored memory to skip files that could not possibly contain a match, without opening and reading them. This unit is only responsible for finding/creating/opening that on-disk memory file and for translating a search pattern into fragments to look up; it does not walk directories or perform the line-by-line search itself. It must never silently use a stale or wrong index in a way that would cause a real match to be missed, and because it is unstable it must not run unless the user explicitly opts in.

units.name: cli-support
units.role: Provides small, well-tested operating-system-facing utilities (running external decompression commands, reading patterns from files/stdin, resolving hostnames, buffered/colored stdout, human-readable size parsing, and byte-string escaping) that the ripgrep application and its flag-parsing layer build on.
units.description: This unit is a toolbox of low-level helpers for talking to the computer's operating system on ripgrep's behalf. It knows how to launch an external program (like gzip or xz) and stream its output back so ripgrep can search inside compressed files; how to read a list of search patterns from a file or from piped-in text; how to find the computer's hostname; how to print colored, properly buffered text to the terminal; how to turn a human-friendly size like '2M' into an exact byte count; and how to turn odd or unprintable bytes into a readable form for error messages. None of it knows anything about searching text itself -- it exists purely so the rest of ripgrep does not have to deal with these operating-system details directly.

It exists so that any other part of ripgrep can report a problem (like an unreadable file or a broken ignore rule) in one consistent, non-interleaved way, without needing to know how the terminal is being used elsewhere.

units.name: cli-flags
units.role: Defines ripgrep's entire command-line surface, parses argv plus config-file arguments into validated settings, and acts as the composition root that assembles the directory walker, regex/PCRE2 matcher, searcher, and printer from those settings.
units.description: This is ripgrep's command-line interface. It knows about every flag and option rg accepts (things like -i, --glob, --json, --sort), turns whatever the user typed (plus anything found in an optional config file) into a raw, low-level set of settings, validates and reconciles those settings into a single high-level configuration object, and generates the --help text, man page, and shell tab-completion scripts. Crucially, this unit does not itself search files or print results -- it only figures out what the user wants and hands out ready-made builder objects (for walking directories, compiling the search pattern, scanning file contents, and formatting output) that other parts of the program use to actually do the work. If you change what a flag does or add a new flag, this is where that change lives.

units.name: search-orchestrator
units.role: Top-level control flow of the rg binary: takes the already-validated settings, decides which mode to run, drives the filesystem walk, wraps each candidate file as a Haystack, dispatches it through a per-thread search worker, aggregates stats/errors, and picks the final process exit code.
units.description: This is the conductor of ripgrep. Once the command-line options have been read and understood elsewhere, this part actually runs the search: it walks through files and folders, decides which ones are worth looking at, hands each one to a worker that applies the pattern and prints results, keeps a running tally of matches and errors, and finally reports back to the operating system whether the run succeeded, found nothing, or hit an error. It does not decide what any given flag means and it does not itself know how to compile a regular expression or read the ignore-file rules; it just wires those pieces together and keeps the books.

entrypoints.name: main
entrypoints.plain: The OS-level process entry point; this is where the rg binary actually starts running.

entrypoints.name: HaystackBuilder
entrypoints.plain: Decides which directory entries are worth searching; configured by the cli-flags unit and driven by main.rs.

entrypoints.name: Haystack
entrypoints.plain: The 'thing to search' value type; also produced/consumed by the cli-flags unit's sort logic.

entrypoints.name: SearchWorkerBuilder
entrypoints.plain: Assembles the matcher+searcher+printer combo that actually runs a search on one file; configured by the cli-flags unit.

effects.description: Opens the target file directly to feed it to an external preprocessor command (crates/core/search.rs).
Spawns an external preprocessing command (--pre) and, via decompression, external decompression binaries for compressed files (crates/core/search.rs).
Measures elapsed search time with Instant::now() for the stats summary (crates/core/main.rs).
Writes search results, file lists, and generated docs/help/version text to stdout; spawns OS threads and uses channels to search and print concurrently (crates/core/main.rs).

violations_observed.note: HiArgs::haystack_builder() and HiArgs::search_worker() (cli-flags) directly construct HaystackBuilder and SearchWorkerBuilder, which are owned by search-orchestrator's files (haystack.rs, search.rs). Both types are legitimate public constructors (not private internals), but this creates a genuine two-way coupling: search-orchestrator's main.rs calls back into HiArgs to obtain configured walkers/matchers/searchers/printers, while cli-flags' hiargs.rs reaches forward into search-orchestrator's own builder types to construct them. This is an intentional composition-root pattern (HiArgs acts as the wiring point for the whole application) rather than an accident, but it means these two units are not cleanly layered -- a reviewer wanting a strict one-directional dependency graph would need to move HaystackBuilder/SearchWorkerBuilder's construction logic into cli-flags itself, or move the mode-dispatch logic in hiargs.rs out of it. Recorded, not fixed.
